The title pretty much says it all. I've had nothing but problems with cloudflare ever since I set it up. For the last few days I have been completely unable to reach pixeldrain through cloudflare, that was the last straw. The only thing that was holding me back was that after removing cloudflare all https links would stop working, so I had to do a seamless transition to letsencrypt, which was not easy to do without downtime. You may have noticed that the website was very unstable yesterday.

The webserver that I use, Apache Tomcat, doesn't support SSL certificates very well, and setting it up is a complete pain in the butt. So I went with the nginx reverse proxy route instead, which also gives the benefit of supporting the http/2 protocol. Double win!

I haven't been able to update the website for a long time due to a shortage of time. Some personal stuff was getting in the way of my productivity, super frustrating. But now I've finished all of it and my creativity may flow freely again. Expect some changes in the near(-ish) future. But remember that I still have a fulltime job which takes up a lot of time too.

Summary:

  • You can now upload files up to 5 GB without switching to (insecure) http.
  • Pixeldrain will automatically switch to https when trying to open a http connection.
  • HTTP/2 support for improved performance.
  • More time for developing new features.
2017-07-20 Replaced cloudflare with nginx proxy. Finally installed letsencrypt. Uploading to "direct.pixeldra.in" no longer required.
Awesome! Glad you found some more time to work on it. What sort of bandwidth are you hosting these days? Is it still (more or less) breaking even?

Currently the website is serving about 6 TiB/month, and it's growing at a steady pace. The system administrator has been managing the machine as a kind of charity, the machine has been running in his colocation centre for over a year and he has never charged me, despite being the biggest bandwidth hog in the entire building. He has been experimenting with new internet service providers to keep up with the traffic demands.

I've made it clear that I don't mind paying for bandwidth, as long as it doesn't become seriously expensive. I don't mind paying a little bit from my pocket either.

Overall it hasn't cost me anything yet so far, but I expect to start paying soon, as bandwidth keeps growing.
